description_full: Photronics, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture and sale of photomask products and services in the United States, Taiwan, China, Korea, Europe, and internationally. It offers photomasks that are used in the manufacture of integrated circuits and flat panel displays (FPDs); and to transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers, and FDP substrates. The company also provides electrical and optical components. It sells its products to semiconductor and FPD designers, manufacturers, and foundries through its sales personnel and customer service representatives. The company was formerly known as Photronic Labs, Inc. and changed its name to Photronics, Inc. in 1990. Photronics, Inc. was incorporated in 1969 and is based in Brookfield, Connecticut.
ceo_bio: Mr. George C. Macricostas | CEO & Executive Chairman | Age 55 | Compensation: $1.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $445K ranks in the above the sector median among Technology peers. Each employee generates $31K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $7K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Photronics, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $1.6B market cap on $849M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 34% against a 12% cost of capital — a 22-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 25% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $60M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.82× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 37× is fortress-like.
Management returns a meaningful 6.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 3.2% of the shares.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 25% operating margin runs 18pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.05x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 36% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 20% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 51% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 83% and a beta of 1.36, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.95 vs 5y 1.72), so read it loosely.
About $23.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 97% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 37% below its DCF fair value of $43.27, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $29.07 to $66.21 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 9.7 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 4.7 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 25% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 16.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $41.33 on average, 51% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 34% clears the cost of capital of 11.5% by 22pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.80).
It runs a 25% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.82x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 8pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.9% of revenue on R&D and 1.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $588.2M (36% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.0% over 3 years, 6.9% over 5 years and 4.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 16.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.4x depreciation (22.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.2%, and institutions hold 97%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $5.8M sold).
It returns 6.0% a year to shareholders (6.0% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 0.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 1,908 employees, each generates about $445K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 3.7% a year.
That works out to $31K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.2M (3x revenue per employee).
